<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">The BrowserGym ecosystem addresses the growing need for efficient evaluation and benchmarking of web agents, particularly those leveraging automation and Large Language Models (LLMs) for web interaction tasks. Many existing benchmarks suffer from fragmentation and inconsistent evaluation methodologies, making it challenging to achieve reliable comparisons and reproducible results. In an earlier work, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Drouin et al. (2024)</a></cite> introduced BrowserGym which aims to solve this by providing a unified, gym-like environment with well-defined observation and action spaces, facilitating standardized evaluation across diverse benchmarks. We propose an extended BrowserGym-based ecosystem for web agent research, which unifies existing benchmarks from the literature and includes AgentLab, a complementary framework that aids in agent creation, testing, and analysis. Our proposed ecosystem offers flexibility for integrating new benchmarks while ensuring consistent evaluation and comprehensive experiment management. This standardized approach seeks to reduce the time and complexity of developing web agents, supporting more reliable comparisons and facilitating in-depth analysis of agent behaviors, and could result in more adaptable, capable agents, ultimately accelerating innovation in LLM-driven automation. As a supporting evidence, we conduct the first large-scale, multi-benchmark web agent experiment and compare the performance of 6 state-of-the-art LLMs across 6 popular web agent benchmarks made available in BrowserGym. Among other findings, our results highlight a large discrepancy between OpenAI and Anthropic’s latests models, with Claude-3.5-Sonnet leading the way on almost all benchmarks, except on vision-related tasks where GPT-4o is superior. Despite these advancements, our results emphasize that building robust and efficient web agents remains a significant challenge, due to the inherent complexity of real-world web environments and the limitations of current models.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In recent years, the emergence of powerful large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Meta, 2024</a>)</cite> has led to a revolution in the field of conversational assistants, otherwise known as chatbots. Since then, the capabilities of these traditional, chat-only assistants have been expanded to include running search queries on the web, reading user documents, executing sand-boxed code, and generating images. Of particular interest in this work is the capability for conversational assistants to perform actions in a web browser on behalf of the user, by directly manipulating its human-facing graphical user interface (UI).</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Many everyday tasks we perform on the web are simple, yet repetitive and time-consuming. Filling out redundant administrative forms, visiting e-commerce websites in search of the best deal, or manually synchronizing different calendars are all tedious tasks that involve multi-step execution. Having autonomous web assistants that can follow instructions and execute such tasks on our behalf would empower users to focus on higher-level, higher-value decisions instead. They also represent a great opportunity to improve digital accessibility, by helping visually or otherwise impaired users who may find certain websites difficult to navigate. Lastly, assistants acting through a UI offer interpretability, since users can visually verify what the agent does on the screen, along with a wide compatibility, bypassing the need to develop specific application programming interfaces (APIs) to adapt existing software for the agentic era. We also note that web agent research is conveniently accessible to LLMs due to the textual modality of the UI, although most research on planning and reasoning with web agents is likely to translate to pixel-based UI agents.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2412.05467v4/agentlab-diagram.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:454/377;" width="454" height="377" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Overview of the ecosystem, including AgentLab, BrowserGym, and the web agent benchmarks.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The field of web agents has been particularly active in the last few years. Most recent works focus on evaluating the capabilities of state-of-the-art LLMs / VLMs at solving tasks of varying difficulty, which has led to an abundance of new web agent benchmarks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib75" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koh et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lù et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Drouin et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Boisvert et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yoran et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pan et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Unfortunately, with this multitude of contributions also comes a multitude of diverging codes for evaluating web agents, which yields research silos with inconsistent practices and incompatible implementations. This fragmentation is detrimental to the fair comparison of existing web agent implementations across benchmarks, which compounds the cumbersome process of installing diverse setups, adapting data formats, and manually incorporating agents into each separate benchmark.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we introduce the BrowserGym ecosystem, highlighted in <a href="#S1.F1" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ The BrowserGym Ecosystem for Web Agent Research" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, which is meant to provide an open, easy-to-use, and extensible framework to accelerate the field of web agent research.<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
            
            
            
            
            
            
            
          It is important to note that this work is meant to provide a research framework, not a consumer product.</span></span></span> It consists of AgentLab, which offers the tooling for building web agents and running large-scale experiments, and a unified collection of web agent benchmarks exposed through BrowserGym <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Drouin et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, which provides the standard interface for web tasks and web agents. In its philosophy, the BrowserGym ecosystem intends to address the three following use cases: a) the design of new web agents, and their straightforward evaluation on a wide range of existing benchmarks; b) the design of new benchmarks, and the straightforward evaluation of existing web agents on them; c) the comparison of different models (LLMs / VLMs) in their ability to solve web agent tasks, by switching the backbone model in a state-of-the-art web agent implementation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We summarize our contributions as follows:</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We expand the existing <span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">BrowserGym<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
                    <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note"><span id="footnote2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">2</span></span>
                    
                    
                    
                    
                    
                    
                    
                  <a href="https://github.com/ServiceNow/BrowserGym" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_medium">https://github.com/ServiceNow/BrowserGym</a></span></span></span></span> library from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Drouin et al. (2024)</a></cite> (<a href="#S3" title="3 BrowserGym ‣ The BrowserGym Ecosystem for Web Agent Research" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>), and we provide a <span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">unification of existing benchmarks</span> (<a href="#S4" title="4 Unification of Web Agent Benchmarks ‣ The BrowserGym Ecosystem for Web Agent Research" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>) proposed by the scientific community in BrowserGym, ranging from MiniWoB(++) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shi et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2018</a>)</cite> to more recent benchmarks such as AssistantBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yoran et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and VisualWebArena <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koh et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>. Despite their differences, all benchmarks are made available through the same, unified BrowserGym interface.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">AgentLab<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
                    <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note"><span id="footnote3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">3</span></span>
                    
                    
                    
                    
                    
                    
                    
                  <a href="https://github.com/ServiceNow/AgentLab" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_medium">https://github.com/ServiceNow/AgentLab</a></span></span></span></span> (<a href="#S5" title="5 AgentLab ‣ The BrowserGym Ecosystem for Web Agent Research" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>), a set of tools to simplify parallel large-scale experimentation with agents over BrowserGym in a reproducible manner. It also comes with AgentXRay, a visual tool to introspect the behavior of agents on individual tasks. Finally, it provides reusable building blocks to accelerate the development of new agents.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We conduct the first, large-scale <span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">web agent experiment</span> (<a href="#S6" title="6 Experiments ‣ The BrowserGym Ecosystem for Web Agent Research" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>) showcasing the BrowserGym ecosystem. We compare the performance of six state-of-the-art LLMs / VLMs from the GPT-4 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2024a</a>)</cite>, Claude 3.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2024a</a>)</cite> and Llama 3.1 families <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Meta, 2024</a>)</cite> across all web agent benchmarks available in BrowserGym. Among others, these results highlight an impressive performance for the new Claude-3.5-Sonnet model, which reaches an unprecedented success rate of 39.1% on the WorkArena L2 benchmark, to be compared with 8.5% for GPT-4o (2nd place). These results serve as first entries to the <span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">BrowserGym leaderboard</span>.<span id="footnote4" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup>
                  <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">4</span>
                  
                  
                  
                  
                  
                  
                  
                <a href="https://huggingface.co/spaces/ServiceNow/browsergym-leaderboard" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://huggingface.co/spaces/ServiceNow/browsergym-leaderboard</a></span></span></span></p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Background and Related Works</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The field of autonomous agents has long been a major research interest both in academia and industry, with a recent surge in LLM-based agents <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>, motivated by the emergence of reasoning and planning capabilities in LLMs
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024c</a>)</cite>.
While a large body of work focuses on software control via APIs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2023a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hao et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, another line of research focuses on automating human-like interactions, by directly manipulating UIs on mobile devices <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rawles et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rawles et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, desktops <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bonatti et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and websites <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Furuta et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gur et al., 2023a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Drouin et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lù et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. This last category encompasses the field of <em id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">web agents</em>, which can automate software interaction even in environments without APIs, improve human productivity, and provide accessibility for users with disabilities. Next, we provide an overview of the recent literature related to web agents, which we divide into two parts: web agent benchmarks and web agent implementations.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Web Agent Benchmarks</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given the rapid pace of improvement in the field of Artificial Intelligence (AI), web agent benchmarks have been consistently evolving to evaluate more and more complex capabilities.
Early benchmarks such as MiniWoB and MiniWoB++ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shi et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2018</a>)</cite> established foundational metrics for evaluating basic web interactions like form filling and button clicking in controlled environments.
WebShop <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2022a</a>)</cite> later introduced complex e-commerce scenarios, requiring agents to navigate product catalogs while considering user preferences and constraints. Mind2Web <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al., 2023</a>)</cite> further expanded this scope and released a dataset of over 2,000 human traces collected from open-ended tasks across 137 real-world websites, along with a structured approach to evaluate multi-step interactions to develop and evaluate generalist web agents. WebVoyager <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al., 2024</a>)</cite> proposed a live, online benchmark for evaluating web agents on real-world tasks from 15 popular websites. WebCanvas <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pan et al., 2024</a>)</cite> later extended Mind2Web from a static dataset to an online benchmark called Mind2Web-Live, by proposing a key-node evaluation mechanism for web agents.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">WebArena <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib75" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>, along with its counterparts VisualWebArena <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koh et al., 2024a</a>)</cite> and VideoWebArena <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, brought innovation by testing agents on live websites rather than simulated environments. This approach evaluated agents’ abilities to handle real-world variability in website design and the dynamic nature of the content. VisualWebArena specifically addressed the role of visual understanding in modern web interfaces by introducing evaluation tasks that require interpreting and manipulating visual content across e-commerce websites, including product image comparison, visual search, and spatial reasoning about interface layouts.
WebLINX <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lù et al., 2024</a>)</cite> focuses on the instruction-following abilities of agents and provides a dataset of over 100k human interactions across 155 real-world websites. Building in the same direction, AssistantBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yoran et al., 2024</a>)</cite> presents 214 realistic tasks requiring agents to navigate multiple websites to gather and synthesize information. MMInA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024b</a>)</cite> extends this further with 1,050 multimodal tasks that require agents to navigate between multiple websites, specifically evaluating their ability to handle both visual and textual information across naturally compositional tasks. In the same vein, GAIA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mialon et al., 2023</a>)</cite> proposes another question-answering benchmark that requires agents to navigate and combine information from diverse sources of the web to find the correct answer.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">While these benchmarks focus on everyday websites, WorkArena and WorkArena++ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Drouin et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Boisvert et al., 2024</a>)</cite> introduced the first benchmark for web agents in the enterprise software setting, evaluating on common knowledge work tasks following realistic workflow.
CRMArena <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2024a</a>)</cite> proposes nine customer service tasks distributed across three personas: service agent, analyst, and manager, designed to evaluate the abilities of AI agents in CRM systems.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Broader evaluation frameworks like AgentBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2023b</a>)</cite>, AndroidWorld <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rawles et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, OS World <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and Windows Agent Arena <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bonatti et al., 2024</a>)</cite> incorporate web tasks as part of a more general agentic environment, providing insights into more general agent capabilities. These benchmarks explore the intersection of web, desktop, and mobile interfaces, recognizing the increasingly blurred boundaries between user interfaces. Addressing the need for safety evaluation, ST-WebAgentBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Levy et al., 2024</a>)</cite> introduces the first benchmark specifically focused on assessing web agents’ compliance with organizational policies and safety requirements in enterprise settings.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Web Agent Implementations</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Due to their immense potential, there has been a substantial effort in developing web agents. These agents differ in how they interact with the web environment, the backbone models, and the goal they aim to achieve, among others.
Popular approaches either interact directly with HTML elements <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nakano et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gur et al., 2023b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gur et al., 2024</a>)</cite> or
leverage vision-language models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2023a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Meta, 2024</a>)</cite>, by grounding screenshots to web elements <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Furuta et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koh et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kil et al., 2024</a>)</cite> or directly at the pixel-level <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shaw et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cheng et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gou et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Beyond interaction methods, researchers have also explored ways to enhance agent reasoning capabilities through prompting or tuning.
Previous works suggested specialized prompting <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sridhar et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib73" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2024c</a>; <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sarch et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chi et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, planning and search architectures <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib74" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yoran et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koh et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>, and training methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gur et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nakano et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Humphreys et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Putta et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sodhi et al., 2024</a>)</cite> to improve performance.
Due to the recent success of LLM-based agents and the challenging reasoning required, agents often use prompting techniques such as chain-of-thought <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, tree-of-thought <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, ReAct <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2022b</a>)</cite>, and RCI <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2024a)</a></cite> provides a survey of LM-based agents.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Other works focus on introducing frameworks for web agent development, by simplifying access to evaluation datasets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lhoest et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">UK AI Safety Institute, 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, agent development <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, and interaction with live websites <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pan et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>.
It is thus important to focus on standardizing web agents research, aiming to simplify future work, and introducing research best practices—standard evaluation with statistical power across benchmarks, simple ecosystem-growth enabling open-source research, and reproducible experiments at scale. Such a framework is needed not only for the development of the next generation of open-source web agents but also for general tasks that require web access, including the development of autonomous coding agents <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>.
To address those important points, we developed BrowserGym and AgentLab, which we describe in detail in the subsequent sections.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>BrowserGym</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">BrowserGym provides a unified interface for web agents, i.e., conversational assistants that can use a web browser as a tool. As showcased in <a href="#S3.F2" title="In 3 BrowserGym ‣ The BrowserGym Ecosystem for Web Agent Research" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, both the user and the agent have access to a chat where they can exchange messages, and a browser in which they can perform actions, such as typing text, clicking buttons, or opening tabs. The user typically writes instructions in the chat, and the agent tries to follow them by navigating across pages, performing UI actions, extracting information, and writing back messages in the chat.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2412.05467v4/figures/stickman.png" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:454/252;" width="454" height="252" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S3.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">A rendered BrowserGym environment, with the chat on the left and the web browser on the right.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Implementation</h5>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">From the agent’s perspective, this interaction loop can be conceptualized as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP), where the environment (chat and browser) provides the current observation and reward, and the agent produces the next action. BrowserGym environments follow the standard OpenAI Gym API <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brockman et al., 2016</a>)</cite><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Towers et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and are made available in Python through the gymnasium<span id="footnote5" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">5</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            <a href="https://gymnasium.farama.org/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://gymnasium.farama.org/</a></span></span></span> interface (<a href="#S3.F3" title="In Implementation ‣ 3 BrowserGym ‣ The BrowserGym Ecosystem for Web Agent Research" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>). Internally, BrowserGym relies on the Chromium<span id="footnote6" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">6</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">6</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">6</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            <a href="https://www.chromium.org/Home/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://www.chromium.org/Home/</a></span></span></span> browser and the Playwright<span id="footnote7" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">7</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">7</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">7</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            <a href="https://playwright.dev/python/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://playwright.dev/python/</a></span></span></span> library to automate browser interactions.</p>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Extensive Observation Space</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">BrowserGym provides a rich observation space, with its main components being the task’s goal (or chat history), the list of open tabs, and the current page’s content.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S3.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Different visual and text representations of the current page from BrowserGym.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Structured page description</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">BrowserGym provides the raw DOM (Document Object Model; <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeauthor"><a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Web Hypertext Application Technology Working Group</a></cite>, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeyear"><a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">2024</a></cite>) and the AXTree (accessibility tree; <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeauthor"><a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">World Wide Web Consortium</a></cite>, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeyear"><a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">2017</a></cite>) as structured representations of the current page, which are extracted using the Chrome Developer Protocol (CDP). They are both provided as-is (<span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">dom_object</span>, <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">axtree_object</span>) with only minimal alterations such as the injection of unique identifier attribute (<span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">bid</span>, see next paragraph). It is then left for the web agent implementation to decide how to further process and format these observations, for example by filtering irrelevant elements or attributes and converting the DOM or AXTree to a suitable text format for LLM-based text agents (see <a href="#S3.F4.sf3" title="In Figure 4 ‣ 3.1 Extensive Observation Space ‣ 3 BrowserGym ‣ The BrowserGym Ecosystem for Web Agent Research" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figures</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4(c)</span></a> and <a href="#S3.F4.sf4" title="Figure 4(d) ‣ Figure 4 ‣ 3.1 Extensive Observation Space ‣ 3 BrowserGym ‣ The BrowserGym Ecosystem for Web Agent Research" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4(d)</span></a>). Utility functions that convert these objects to basic text representation are also provided, for implementing simple agents quickly.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Extra element properties</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">BrowserGym enriches each HTML element in the current webpage with extra information to facilitate web agent interactions. One key property is the BrowserGym ID (<span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">bid</span>), a uniquely-generated, element-wise identifier injected into the page’s DOM and AXTree, allowing for unambiguous interaction with the elements of the page. To add information about the visual rendering of the page, BrowserGym also provides for each element its bounding box coordinates (<span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">bbox</span>) in the form of a <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\text{left, top, width, height})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>left, top, width, height</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\text{left, top, width, height})</annotation></semantics></math> 4-tuple, as well as its visibility ratio<span id="footnote8" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">8</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">8</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">8</span>
                
                
                
                
                
                
                
              <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Intersection_Observer_API" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Intersection_Observer_API</a></span></span></span> (<span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">visibility</span>) in the form of a scalar between 0 and 1. Finally, BrowserGym also provides a Set-of-Marks boolean indicator (<span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">set_of_marks</span>) reproduced from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al. (2024)</a></cite>, which indicates if an element’s bounding box should be overlayed on the screenshot to enable Set-of-Marks prompting <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2023b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. (see <a href="#S3.F4.sf1" title="In Figure 4 ‣ 3.1 Extensive Observation Space ‣ 3 BrowserGym ‣ The BrowserGym Ecosystem for Web Agent Research" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figures</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4(a)</span></a> and <a href="#S3.F4.sf2" title="Figure 4(b) ‣ Figure 4 ‣ 3.1 Extensive Observation Space ‣ 3 BrowserGym ‣ The BrowserGym Ecosystem for Web Agent Research" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4(b)</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Screenshot</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While the DOM, AXTree, and extra element properties provide a rich description of the page’s content, they do not give the full picture of how the page is being rendered in the browser, i.e., overlapping elements, background colors, image contents, fonts, etc. Therefore, BrowserGym also provides the raw <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">screenshot</span> of the current page as part of the observation, in the form of an RGB image. Again, it is up to the agent implementation to decide how to process and use this visual information. Note that the <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">bbox</span> coordinates in the extra element properties map exactly to pixel coordinates in the screenshot, which makes it extremely easy for agents to overlay the bounding boxes and identifiers of relevant elements on the screenshot as in Set-of-Mark prompting <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2023b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Open tabs</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In BrowserGym, tasks can use multiple tabs if needed. While the main focus is on the current page (screenshot and page description), agents are also made aware of all the open browser pages, which include tabs and pop-up windows. BrowserGym’s observations therefore include a list of all the pages’ URLs and titles (<span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">open_pages_urls</span>, <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">open_pages_titles</span>), as well as an index to distinguish the currently active page (<span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">active_page_index</span>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Goal and chat messages</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In BrowserGym web agents can extract the user instructions in two ways, either explicitly from the task goal (<span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">goal_object</span>) or implicitly from the chat (<span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">chat_messages</span>). Both consist of a list of text and/or image messages. This duality is offered to facilitate compatibility with legacy web agent and web task implementations, which do not account for an interactive chat in their design. Note however that BrowserGym will always inject the goal of a non-interactive task in the chat to mimic user interaction, but will not inject further chat messages received during a task execution back into the goal. While, to this date, all web agent benchmarks in the literature are non-interactive, it is preferable to implement web agents using <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">chat_messages</span>, at the very least to be able to record live, interactive demos.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Error feedback</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, BrowserGym observations always include the error message of the last executed action, if any (<span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">last_action_error</span>). Typical errors include trying to interact with an element that is hidden or deactivated, which results in a Playwright exception with an error message. Such exceptions do not break the interaction loop but are instead captured, and are sent back to the agent as part of the next observation. This immediate negative feedback gives web agents a chance to quickly self-correct in the next step (See <a href="#S3.F5" title="In Error feedback ‣ 3.1 Extensive Observation Space ‣ 3 BrowserGym ‣ The BrowserGym Ecosystem for Web Agent Research" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F5" class="ltx_figure">

<div id="lstnumberx32" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx32.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">button</span><span id="lstnumberx32.2" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span>=<span id="lstnumberx32.3" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span><span id="lstnumberx32.4" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">page</span>.<span id="lstnumberx32.5" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">locator</span>(<span id="lstnumberx32.6" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_string">"form"</span>).<span id="lstnumberx32.7" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_keyword ltx_lst_keywords2 ltx_font_bold">filter</span>(<span id="lstnumberx32.8" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">has_text</span>=<span id="lstnumberx32.9" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_string">"17705"</span>)<span id="lstnumberx32.10" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span>.<span id="lstnumberx32.11" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">get_by_role</span>(<span id="lstnumberx32.12" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_string">"button"</span>).<span id="lstnumberx32.13" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">first</span>
</div>
<div id="lstnumberx33" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx33.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">button</span>.<span id="lstnumberx33.2" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">click</span>()
</div>
<div id="lstnumberx34" class="ltx_listingline">
</div>
<div id="lstnumberx35" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx35.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_comment ltx_font_italic">#<span id="lstnumberx35.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span>or,<span id="lstnumberx35.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span>do<span id="lstnumberx35.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span>it<span id="lstnumberx35.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span>in<span id="lstnumberx35.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span>Javascript</span>
</div>

</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F6.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span id="S3.F6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Different BrowserGym actions for clicking the “Upvote” button of the first post in <a href="#S3.F4" title="In 3.1 Extensive Observation Space ‣ 3 BrowserGym ‣ The BrowserGym Ecosystem for Web Agent Research" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. While raw Python code (<a href="#S3.F6.sf1" title="Figure 6(a) ‣ Figure 6 ‣ Error feedback ‣ 3.1 Extensive Observation Space ‣ 3 BrowserGym ‣ The BrowserGym Ecosystem for Web Agent Research" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6(a)</span></a>) enables expressive actions using Playwright or Javascript, it often relies on some knowledge of the page’s HTML structure. Using BrowserGym’s high-level action primitives (<a href="#S3.F6.sf2" title="Figure 6(b) ‣ Figure 6 ‣ Error feedback ‣ 3.1 Extensive Observation Space ‣ 3 BrowserGym ‣ The BrowserGym Ecosystem for Web Agent Research" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6(b)</span></a>) is more restrictive but offers more control over what the agent can do and how it should interact with the browser.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Expandable Action Space</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The fundamental action space of BrowserGym is raw executable Python code (<a href="#S3.F6.sf1" title="In Figure 6 ‣ Error feedback ‣ 3.1 Extensive Observation Space ‣ 3 BrowserGym ‣ The BrowserGym Ecosystem for Web Agent Research" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6(a)</span></a>). Agents have access to a Playwright <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">page</span> object along with two functions <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">send_message_to_user(text)</span> and <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">report_infeasible(reason)</span>. These respectively allow agents to interact with the browser, and the chat, and terminate the task. This design choice offers a powerful, unrestricted action space for researchers to play with, but also exposes web agent users to vulnerabilities and safety risks due to the possibility of executing arbitrary, untrusted code. To mitigate this, BrowserGym offers a control mechanism to further restrict the action space available to web agents, through the use of an <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">action_mapping</span> function.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Action mapping</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In BrowserGym, users can instantiate environments with an optional <span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">action_mapping</span> function, which the environment uses to convert input actions into executable Python code. It is then easy to define and experiment with new, custom action spaces in BrowserGym, for example by allowing a pre-defined list of actions in JSON or in command-line format, which are parsed and converted to safe, trusted Python code. In case of a conversion error (e.g., parsing errors), any Exception message raised by <span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">action_mapping()</span> is caught and fed back to the agent as an error feedback.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">High-level action set</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">By default, BrowserGym environments use a pre-defined action mapping (<a href="#S3.F6.sf2" title="In Figure 6 ‣ Error feedback ‣ 3.1 Extensive Observation Space ‣ 3 BrowserGym ‣ The BrowserGym Ecosystem for Web Agent Research" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6(b)</span></a>), which converts a set of high-level action primitives in the form of function calls into actual Playwright code to be executed. An exhaustive list of these primitives can be found in <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A BrowserGym’s High-Level Action Set ‣ The BrowserGym Ecosystem for Web Agent Research" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>, <a href="#A1.T3" title="In Appendix A BrowserGym’s High-Level Action Set ‣ The BrowserGym Ecosystem for Web Agent Research" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. The resulting action set is encapsulated in the <span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">HighLevelActionSet</span> class, which provides a <span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">to_python_code()</span> method for the environment (the action mapping), and a <span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">describe()</span> method for the agent, which builds a textual description of the available high-level primitives and how to use them (<a href="#A1" title="Appendix A BrowserGym’s High-Level Action Set ‣ The BrowserGym Ecosystem for Web Agent Research" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>, <a href="#A1.F10" title="In Appendix A BrowserGym’s High-Level Action Set ‣ The BrowserGym Ecosystem for Web Agent Research" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">

<div id="lstnumberx67" class="ltx_listingline">
</div>
<div id="lstnumberx68" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx68.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_comment ltx_font_italic">#<span id="lstnumberx68.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span>available<span id="lstnumberx68.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span>as<span id="lstnumberx68.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span>a<span id="lstnumberx68.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span>gym<span id="lstnumberx68.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span>environment</span>
</div>
<div id="lstnumberx69" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx69.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">env</span><span id="lstnumberx69.2" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span>=<span id="lstnumberx69.3" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span><span id="lstnumberx69.4" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">gym</span>.<span id="lstnumberx69.5" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">make</span>(<span id="lstnumberx69.6" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_string">"browsergym/mynewtask"</span>)
</div>
</div>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S3.F7.fig2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2412.05467v4/figures/my_new_task.png" id="S3.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:648/368;" width="648" height="368" alt="Refer to caption">
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F7.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 7</span>: </span><span id="S3.F7.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Pseudo-code for creating a simple web task in BrowserGym, and the corresponding rendering.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">BrowserGym minimizes the effort needed for practitioners to implement new web tasks. Doing so only requires writing the logic of the task, which takes the form of a <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">setup()</span> and a <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">validate()</span> method.</p>
<ul id="S3.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Setup</span> Starting from a blank <span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">page</span> object, this method must bring the browser to the starting point of the task, and return the goal the web agent must achieve. This will typically involve logging into a system, creating data entries if needed, and navigating to a task-specific starting URL. Then, the method must return a goal which can either be a raw string as in <a href="#S3.F7" title="In 3.3 Extensibility: create your own task ‣ 3 BrowserGym ‣ The BrowserGym Ecosystem for Web Agent Research" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> or a list of OpenAI-style messages<span id="footnote9" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">9</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">9</sup>
                    <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">9</span>
                    
                    
                    
                    
                    
                    
                    
                  <a href="https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/messages" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/messages</a></span></span></span> that can include text and images, to allow for vision-conditioned goals (e.g., “Find a pair of shoes that look like this image”).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Validate</span> Called after each agent action is executed, this method must check whether the agent has completed the task. It has access to the current state of the browser through the active <span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">page</span>, as well as the history of <span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">chat_messages</span> which contains all previous user and assistant messages. Typical validation steps involve looking at the content of the current page, searching for database entries and updates, or reading assistant messages in the chat in search of a correct answer. At the end, this method must produce a scalar <span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">reward</span> for the agent, a boolean <span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">done</span> flag that indicates task termination, and an optional <span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">message</span> to be added to the chat, to simulate user interaction.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Unification of Web Agent Benchmarks</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We bring 3 new web agent benchmarks to BrowserGym, namely WebLINX <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lù et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, VisualWebArena <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koh et al., 2024a</a>)</cite> and AssistantBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yoran et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. With these, BrowserGym currently supports six popular web agent benchmarks, listed in <a href="#S4.T1" title="In 4 Unification of Web Agent Benchmarks ‣ The BrowserGym Ecosystem for Web Agent Research" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. Each benchmark consists of a set of BrowserGym tasks, accessible as a BrowserGym environment through the gymnasium interface (<a href="#S4.F8" title="In 4 Unification of Web Agent Benchmarks ‣ The BrowserGym Ecosystem for Web Agent Research" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>).
Any task from any of these benchmarks can then be executed using the same code base, through the same observation/action API, and any web agent implemented for one benchmark can readily be evaluated on another.<span id="footnote10" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">10</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">10</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">10</span>
            
            
            
            
            
            
            
          BrowserGym also suggests a unified API for agent creation which streamlines implementation efforts (<a href="#S5.SS5" title="5.5 Extensibility: create your own agent ‣ 5 AgentLab ‣ The BrowserGym Ecosystem for Web Agent Research" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.5</span></a>).</span></span></span> The advantages are the following:</p>
<ul id="S4.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Breaking silos</span>. Unifying benchmarks encourages the development of general-purpose web agents. While benchmark-specific solutions have their own merit <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sodhi et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and correspond to real use cases (e.g., a company developing a web agent for an internal website), we believe that the pursuit of generic solutions is more likely to bring long-term, impactful innovation.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Accelerating research</span>. Proposing a unified interface for web agents will also encourage the development of new, compatible benchmarks, stimulate progress in the field, and accelerate research. For example, a new BrowserGym-compatible security benchmark could easily evaluate all existing web agent implementations, without the need to spend time and effort adapting agent codes.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Reducing noise</span>. By evaluating across benchmarks, practitioners can collect stronger statistical signals for testing design choices and scientific hypotheses. Does using screenshots improve the performance of web agents? Is LLM-A a better web agent than LLM-B? Evaluating on a single benchmark with its own biases and specificities only provides a partial answer, while cross-benchmark evaluation gives a wider picture.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F8" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">

<td id="S4.T1.5.2.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T1.5.2.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">self-hosted pages</span></td>
<td id="S4.T1.5.2.7" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T1.5.2.7.1" class="ltx_text"></span><span id="S4.T1.5.2.7.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> <span id="S4.T1.5.2.7.2.1" class="ltx_text">
<span id="S4.T1.5.2.7.2.1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<span id="S4.T1.5.2.7.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S4.T1.5.2.7.2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shi et al. (2017)</a></cite></span></span>
